analysis.one_liner: Requires defense contractors to prove their costs and publicly disclose profit margins and pricing strategies.
analysis.headline: Introduced by a Democratic and a Republican senator, the bill sat in the Senate Armed Services Committee for about 18 months, never got a hearing or vote, and died when the Congress ended in January 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have forced companies selling weapons, goods, and services to the Pentagon to open their books: certified cost data on sole-source and cost-reimbursement deals, fewer ways to dodge scrutiny by labeling products "commercial," faster government payments only for contractors that share pricing information, and annual public reports on price increases, profit margins, and pricing strategy. Its aim was to stop defense contractors from raising prices faster than their costs rose and billing taxpayers for the difference.
analysis.who_benefits: Taxpayers, who fund the largest procurement budget in the world and currently absorb price increases on contracts where contractors face little or no competition. Pentagon contracting officers would get certified cost data and margin disclosures to negotiate with, and the public could read the annual pricing reports. Contractors that play by the rules would compete on a more level field against firms that pad prices.

how_it_helps.text: Would require companies seeking sole-source or cost-reimbursement Pentagon contracts to certify their actual cost or pricing data, closing a rule that let single-bid deals skip that step entirely.

Would narrow the 'commercial item' exemption contractors use to avoid showing their costs, by removing items merely 'offered for sale' and requiring proof of actual sales in 'like quantities' rather than vaguely defined 'substantial quantities'.

Would require traditional defense contractors to report annually how much their prices, costs, and gross margins changed, and to explain in writing any decision to raise prices faster than costs — with the reports published on a public website.

Would run a pilot tying faster government progress payments to a contractor's willingness to provide certified cost or pricing data within 30 days, so speed of payment rewards transparency instead of stonewalling.

analysis.who_pays: Large defense contractors. They would bear compliance costs, face capped progress payments (a baseline of 50 percent instead of faster rates) that raise their financing costs, lose the ability to rely on 'commercial item' carve-outs to skip cost disclosure, and have their margins and pricing rationale published for the public, their rivals, and reporters to see. Some of that cost could be passed back through prices or by slowing deliveries.

drawbacks.text: The pilot would cap progress payments for traditional contractors at 50 percent — well below the standard federal rate of around 80 percent for large businesses — forcing contractors to finance production out of their own cash or borrow, a cost that could hit smaller subcontractors in the supply chain hardest and get passed into prices.

Narrowing the 'commercial item' definition reverses a decades-long reform effort to speed defense buying through commercial-style procedures; stricter definitions and mandatory cost data could slow routine purchases and add paperwork to ordinary transactions.

Publishing contractors' detailed margins, cost breakdowns, and pricing strategies on a public website would hand competitively sensitive business information to rivals, including foreign competitors, which contractors would argue weakens their position in negotiations and export markets.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core of the bill is disclosure: the Pentagon and the public would finally see whether prices are rising faster than costs on the hundreds of billions spent annually, and contractors would have to justify it when they are. The real costs are compliance paperwork and tighter payment terms for contractors — real, but modest next to the sums at stake, and the payment terms carry an exception that restores faster rates for any contractor that cooperates within 30 days. The public-disclosure provision is the bluntest instrument and could slow some routine buying, but an honest reading is that the transparency gains likely outweigh the friction. The main cost of the bill is that it never happened: no one had to test the balance.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate Armed Services Committee never took the bill up, and it died when the 118th Congress ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: Senator Elizabeth Warren introduced the Stop Pentagon Price Gouging Act on June 20, 2023, joined by Republican Senator Mike Braun, giving it bipartisan sponsorship from the start.
The Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Armed Services Committee the same day; the only later action was a 'star print' — a routine reprint of the bill — on July 19, 2023.
In the roughly 18 months that followed, the committee held no hearing, no markup, and no vote on the bill, and the full Senate never considered it before the Congress ended on January 3, 2025.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Large defense contractors came out ahead: they avoided tighter cost disclosure, narrower 'commercial item' carve-outs, capped progress payments, and annual public reporting of margins and pricing strategy. Taxpayers gained nothing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Big defense contractors, spared price scrutiny

for.name: Elizabeth Warren
for.role: U.S. Senator (D-MA); member of the Senate Armed Services Committee
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on June 20, 2023 and drafted its provisions tightening cost-data rules, narrowing the commercial item exemption, and mandating public contractor pricing reports.

for.name: Mike Braun
for.what_they_did: Joined Warren as the bill's co-introducer, giving it bipartisan sponsorship; the cosponsor record lists one Republican cosponsor.

against.name: Senate Armed Services Committee
against.role: Committee of referral, chaired by Sen. Jack Reed (D-RI)
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral on June 20, 2023 and never scheduled a hearing or markup; the only follow-on action in the record was a routine star print, leaving the bill to die with the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: A Democrat and a Republican introduced the bill together, but with no hearing, markup, or floor vote ever held, the record shows no way to know how the parties would have lined up.

industries.industry: Traditional defense contractors (weapons, systems, and services makers)
industries.note: The bill hits this group from four directions: mandatory certified cost data on sole-source and cost-reimbursement deals, a narrower 'commercial item' exemption that currently lets them skip cost scrutiny, progress payments capped at 50 percent unless they hand over pricing data within 30 days, and annual public reports on price hikes, gross margins, and pricing strategy. Its interest in avoiding price scrutiny runs directly against taxpayers who pay the bills.

The payment restrictions and reporting duties apply only to 'traditional contractors' with a track record of Pentagon work; new entrants and universities are exempt, giving them a relative edge in bidding and cash flow if the bill passed.
